lessons.title: Milking hygienically
lessons.html:
Milking hygienically

Milk is a food. It spoils quickly and can carry germs that make people sick. Clean milking gives safe milk, a better price from the buyer and healthier cows.

Before milking

  • Wash your hands and arms with soap. Wear clean overalls, an apron and gloves.
  • Keep fingernails short. Cover cuts on your hands.
  • Do not milk if you have diarrhoea or an infected wound; tell your supervisor.
  • Check that the milking machine, buckets and the bulk tank are clean.
  • Bring cows in calmly. Stressed cows do not let down their milk well.

Milking steps

  1. Fore-strip: squeeze two or three streams from each teat into a strip cup. Look for clots, blood or watery milk. These are signs of mastitis (udder infection).
  2. Clean the teats: use a pre-dip or clean, wet paper towel, one per cow. Dry the teats well.
  3. Attach the cups soon after cleaning, while the cow is letting down milk. Avoid air leaks.
  4. Watch the milking. Remove the cups when the milk flow stops. Over-milking damages teats.
  5. Post-dip: dip each teat in teat dip straight after milking to prevent mastitis.

Milk that must not go into the tank

  • Milk from cows with mastitis.
  • Milk from cows treated with antibiotics or other medicines, until the withdrawal period on the label or from the vet has passed. These cows must be clearly marked, for example with leg bands, and milked last into a separate bucket.
  • Colostrum (first milk after calving) is fed to calves.

After milking

  • Cool the milk quickly in the bulk tank to the temperature set by the buyer.
  • Wash and sanitise the machine and equipment as the cleaning procedure says.
  • Record the milk volume and any sick cows.

lessons.title: Collecting and handling eggs
lessons.html:
Collecting and handling eggs

Eggs are a valuable product on many small and large farms. They break easily and can carry germs such as Salmonella on the shell, so careful handling is important.

Collecting eggs

  • Collect eggs at least twice a day, or as often as the farm schedule says. Eggs left in the nest get dirty, cracked or eaten by hens.
  • Wash your hands before collecting.
  • Use clean egg trays or baskets. Put eggs in with the pointed end down.
  • Handle gently. Do not drop or knock eggs together.
  • Keep the nests clean with fresh nesting material, so eggs stay clean.

Sorting (grading)

  1. Remove cracked, broken, very dirty and misshapen eggs. Put them aside as the farm instructs; do not sell cracked eggs as table eggs.
  2. Lightly soiled eggs may be dry-cleaned with a clean cloth or sandpaper. Follow farm rules on washing; wrong washing can push germs into the egg.
  3. Sort eggs by size or mass as the buyer requires, for example medium, large and extra large.
  4. Pack into clean trays or boxes, pointed end down.

Storage

  • Store eggs in a cool, clean, dry place away from strong smells, chemicals and direct sun.
  • Use the oldest eggs first (first in, first out).
  • Mark the trays with the date collected.

Records

Write down the number of eggs collected per house each day, and the number of cracked or rejected eggs. A sudden drop in eggs can be an early sign of disease, heat stress, feed or water problems. Report it.

Hygiene for workers

Wash your hands after handling hens, eggs and manure, and before eating. Wear the clothing and boots the farm provides, and use the foot bath at the door of the poultry house.

lessons.title: Shearing, wool and other products
lessons.html:
Shearing, wool and other products

South Africa produces wool from Merino and other sheep, and mohair from Angora goats, mostly in the Eastern Cape, Free State, Karoo and Northern Cape. Shearing is skilled work done by trained shearers, usually in a shearing shed. Other workers help in the shed.

Getting ready for shearing

  • Sheep must be dry. Wet wool cannot be pressed or stored; it rots and can even catch fire.
  • Keep sheep off feed for some hours before shearing, as the farm instructs, so they are more comfortable on the board.
  • Clean the shearing board and the wool table. Remove twine, plastic and stones.

Jobs in the shearing shed

  1. Catching pens: keep sheep ready for the shearers, calmly.
  2. Picking up the fleece: gather the fleece in one piece and throw it on the wool table, outside down.
  3. Skirting: remove dirty edges, stained wool and belly wool.
  4. Classing: the wool classer sorts fleeces by length, strength, fineness and colour. Workers put each class in the right bin.
  5. Pressing: wool is pressed into bales, labelled with the farm brand and class.

Keep wool clean

Wool buyers pay less for wool with contamination. Never let polypropylene twine, plastic, hair, paint or dung get into the wool. One piece of plastic can spoil a whole bale.

Caring for shorn sheep

  • Treat cuts as instructed.
  • Newly shorn sheep feel the cold badly. Keep them in sheltered camps if cold rain or wind is forecast.

Safety

  • Stay clear of shearing handpieces and moving drive shafts.
  • Lift sheep and bales with your legs, not your back.
  • Keep the floor dry and clear to prevent slips.

Key points

  • Clean hands, clean equipment and fast cooling give safe milk.
  • Never put milk from treated or mastitis cows into the tank; follow the withdrawal period.
  • Collect eggs often, handle gently, remove cracked eggs and store cool.
  • Shear only dry sheep and keep wool free of twine, plastic and dirt.
  • Record production every day; a sudden drop can mean a problem.

quiz.question: Why do you fore-strip a cow before milking?

options.text: To check for clots, blood or watery milk that show mastitis
To fill the bulk tank faster

quiz.question: What must happen to milk from a cow treated with antibiotics?

options.text: Mix it into the bulk tank
Keep it out of the tank until the withdrawal period has passed
Sell it at a lower price
Boil it and put it in the tank

quiz.question: Why is teat dip used straight after milking?

options.text: To make the cow give more milk

quiz.question: How should eggs be placed in a tray?
Why must sheep be dry for shearing?

options.text: Wet wool rots in storage and can catch fire
Wet sheep are heavier to sell
Shearers prefer dry sheep for photos
